summary: The BGP OPEN message carries optional parameters, including capabilities, but a one-octet length field limits them to 255 octets. This document updates RFC 4271 to extend, in a backward-compatible way, the length of the Optional Parameters and of the individual Parameter Length field, addressing concern that capabilities may outgrow the limit.

eli5.summary: A form with a small box for notes can run out of space. This document makes the notes box in a router's hello message bigger, without breaking older routers.

questions: bgp open message optional parameters limit
what is bgp extended optional parameters length
how does bgp handle capabilities longer than 255 octets
subtitle: How a BGP OPEN message escapes the 255-octet limit on its optional parameters without breaking older routers.

tldr.problem: The BGP OPEN message describes its optional parameters with a one-octet length, so they cannot exceed 255 octets. BGP capabilities travel in those parameters and may outgrow the limit.
tldr.mechanism: Optional Parameter type code 255 is reserved as 'Extended Length'. When it appears right after a non-zero one-octet length, a two-octet Extended Optional Parameters Length follows, and each parameter's own length field also becomes two octets.
tldr.outcome: A speaker uses the old encoding whenever the parameters fit in 255 octets. If a new speaker has to send a longer OPEN to an old one, the old speaker rejects it with an OPEN Message Error.

today: RFC 9072 is a Proposed Standard that updates RFC 4271; the metadata lists no RFC that obsoletes or updates it.

sections.title: The 255-Octet Problem
sections.content:
In the base BGP specification (RFC 4271), the Optional Parameters Length field of the OPEN message is one octet. That limits the Optional Parameters field to 255 octets.

BGP capabilities (RFC 5492) are carried in that field, and new capabilities keep being introduced. The limit is therefore a concern for BGP development. RFC 9072 updates RFC 4271 to extend the length in a backward-compatible way.
sections.eli5: The notes box on the form only holds a small number of lines, and people keep wanting to write more. This document finds a way to make room.

sections.title: The Extended OPEN Encoding
sections.content:
The trick is to reserve Optional Parameter type code 255 as Extended Length. In the extended format, the one-octet Non-Extended Optional Parameters Length (Non-Ext OP Len.) is followed by a one-octet Non-Ext OP Type set to 255, and then a two-octet Extended Optional Parameters Length, an unsigned integer giving the total length of the Optional Parameters in octets. A value of zero means no Optional Parameters are present.

The Non-Ext OP Len. field SHOULD be set to 255 on transmission and MUST NOT be set to 0. It MUST be ignored on receipt once the extended format is positively identified by the 255 in the Non-Ext OP Type field.

Each individual Optional Parameter keeps its rules from RFC 4271, except that its Parameter Length field becomes a two-octet unsigned integer.
sections.eli5: The old form has a small box, then a big sticker that says 'use the large box instead', then the size of the large box. Each note inside also gets a bigger size field.

sections.title: When to Use It and How to Parse It
sections.content:
If the Optional Parameters do not exceed 255 octets, the RFC 4271 encoding SHOULD be used unchanged. Configuration MAY force the extended format in all cases, for example to test that a peer supports this specification. In any case, an implementation MUST accept an OPEN message that uses the extended encoding even if the parameters are 255 octets or less. If the parameters do exceed 255, the extended encoding MUST be used.

When parsing, if the one-octet Optional Parameters Length is non-zero, the speaker MUST look at the octet that follows it (Non-Ext OP Type). If it is 255, the extended encoding applies to both the overall length and each parameter's length field. Otherwise the RFC 4271 encoding is used.
sections.eli5: If your notes fit in the small box, just use it. If they do not, put the sticker on. Whoever reads the form checks for the sticker first.

sections.title: Backward Compatibility
sections.content:
No problem arises between a new speaker and an old one unless the new speaker has to send Optional Parameters longer than 255 octets. In that case the old speaker sees what looks like an Optional Parameter of type 255. It does not recognize that type, so it is expected to close the connection with a NOTIFICATION carrying error code OPEN Message Error and subcode Unsupported Optional Parameters, as RFC 4271 Section 6.2 describes.

Type code 255 is not a real Optional Parameter type in the usual sense and MUST NOT be used other than as described. If it appears anywhere except as the Non-Ext OP Type, it MUST be treated as an unrecognized Optional Parameter. It is not an error to receive an extended OPEN whose Extended Optional Parameters Length is 255 or less. It is also not a fatal error to receive an OPEN whose non-extended length is not 255 but whose first parameter type is 255; the extended encoding MUST then be used to decode it.
sections.eli5: An old reader does not know the sticker and says 'I do not understand this form' and hangs up. That only happens when the notes really were too long for the old form.

sections.title: IANA and Security
sections.content:
IANA has assigned value 255 as the Extended Length type code in the 'BGP OPEN Optional Parameter Types' registry.

The security section is a single sentence: the extension does not change the underlying security or confidentiality issues inherent in the existing BGP, which are analyzed in RFC 4272.
sections.eli5: The special sticker number was written down in an official list. The change does not make BGP any safer or less safe than before.
